intro: Researchers often turn to Slovin's formula because it offers a simple way to calculate sample size when they have limited information about their population. It provides a quick, albeit often imprecise, answer for those who lack the time or training for a full power analysis.
tldr: Slovin's formula is popular for its simplicity but lacks the rigor needed for most scientific studies.

blocks.text: The allure of simplicity in sample size determination

You might ask why do researchers use Slovin's formula despite its known limitations. The answer is usually speed and the lack of required parameters. Unlike a formal power analysis that requires you to know your effect size, alpha level, and power, Slovin's formula only asks for the population size and an acceptable margin of error. It feels like a shortcut when you are facing a deadline or lack a background in statistics.
Why Slovin's formula is often a trap

The formula assumes a normal distribution that rarely exists in real world data. It ignores the variance within your population. When you use it, you are likely creating an underpowered study. This means your results will be inconclusive. You might spend weeks or months on data collection only to find that your sample size was too small to detect the effect you are looking for. This is a waste of your time and your institution's money.
How to perform a proper power analysis on your Mac

Instead of relying on simple formulas, use tools designed for statistical rigor. G*Power is the gold standard for many researchers. You can run it on your Mac to calculate the exact sample size needed for your specific test. If you are comfortable with coding, R and RStudio offer even more flexibility. These tools force you to think about your effect size and your tolerance for error before you start recruiting participants.
If you are using G*Power, look for the native Apple Silicon version to ensure it runs efficiently on your Mac. You can find it on their official website.
blocks.title: Use the right tools

faq.question: Is Slovin's formula ever appropriate?
faq.answer: It may be useful for very rough estimates in non-scientific contexts, but it should never be the basis for published research.

faq.question: What should I use instead?
faq.answer: Use a formal power analysis tool like G*Power or R to ensure your study has the statistical power to detect real effects.

costs.title: Wasted time
costs.text: Collecting data that cannot prove your hypothesis is a total loss of time.

costs.title: Financial loss
costs.text: You spend money on participants or software for a study that yields no results.

costs.title: Ethical concerns
costs.text: Involving human subjects in a study that is not powered correctly is ethically questionable.

causes.title: Lack of training
causes.text: Many researchers are not taught how to conduct a proper power analysis.

causes.title: Pressure for speed
causes.text: The need to start a project quickly leads to using the easiest formula available.

causes.title: Over-simplification
causes.text: Assuming that a simple formula can replace complex statistical planning.

fixes.title: Learn power analysis
fixes.text: Take the time to learn how to calculate sample size based on effect size and power.

fixes.title: Use professional software
fixes.text: Download G*Power or install R to perform your calculations.

fixes.title: Consult a statistician
fixes.text: If your study is important, ask a colleague with a statistics background to review your design.
